items.title: L9: Choosing a target grade: stretch or consolidate
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service grades and professions
items.body: Deciding which grade to target is a judgement about evidence, risk and timing. Applying for a role at your current grade is lower risk, builds depth and may be needed to show consistency. Applying one grade up is a stretch: you must show the behaviours at the higher level, which usually means larger scope, more independence, influence over others and accountability for outcomes. A useful test is to read the higher-grade adverts and ask whether you can already give two or three examples at that level, even if informally. If you cannot, you may need a step that builds that evidence, such as a temporary promotion, a project lead role, or a lateral move that brings wider scope. Be cautious about applying only for roles that name the grade you want, since job titles differ between departments. Look at the responsibilities and the success profile. A person with strong evidence but a modest title may be ready, while a person with a long service record but no evidence at the higher level may not be. Avoid a pattern of repeatedly applying for stretch roles without improving evidence between attempts, because repeated rejection does not teach anything on its own. Equally, remaining at the same grade for years without trying a stretch may slow progression. Balance both: apply for a mix, and use each outcome to refine your evidence.

questions.prompt: Which test best shows whether a candidate is ready to apply a grade up?

options.text: Whether they have served a set number of years at their current grade
Whether their line manager has hinted that they might be considered
Whether the job title they want is currently used in their department
Whether they can already give two or three examples at that level

questions.hint: Readiness is about evidence of the higher behaviours, not time or titles.

questions.prompt: Which feature typically marks a higher grade's behaviours compared with the grade below?

options.text: Wider scope, more independence and accountability for outcomes
More frequent use of formal procedures and standard templates
Longer working hours and more frequent deadlines than the grade below
More tasks done under the same level of supervision as before

questions.hint: Higher grades show scope and ownership, not simply more work.

questions.prompt: Hana has strong evidence and a modest job title. Her colleague has twenty years' service but no evidence above the current grade. Who is better placed to apply upward?

options.text: Her colleague, since long service shows commitment and deep knowledge
Hana, since evidence at the higher level matters more than title or service
Neither, because promotion is available only to those nominated by managers
Her colleague, since panels weigh years served before anything else

questions.hint: Merit is judged on evidence of the criteria.

questions.prompt: A candidate applies for stretch roles every month and is rejected each time. What is the main flaw in this strategy?

options.text: Stretch roles are rarely offered to existing civil servants at all
Applying so often is restricted under Civil Service Jobs rules
Repeating the same evidence teaches nothing new
Each rejection lowers the score awarded on later applications

questions.hint: Rejection alone does not improve evidence; build it between attempts.

questions.prompt: Which step would best build evidence for a later promotion?

options.text: Asking for a higher grade without any change in duties
Attending more meetings without a defined contribution to make
Taking on a larger volume of the same routine tasks
Leading a defined project or acting up in a wider role

questions.hint: Scope and ownership build higher-level evidence.

questions.prompt: Why be cautious about searching only for the grade title you want?

options.text: Titles differ between departments, so duties are a better guide
Only adverts with unfamiliar titles are open to internal candidates
Adverts are not allowed to include the grade in the job title
Titles are set nationally, so searching by title is accurate everywhere

questions.hint: Look at duties and the success profile, not the label.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of staying at the same grade for years without ever trying a stretch role?

options.text: Pay is reduced after a set time without a change of role
The person loses access to internal vacancies after three years
Progression may slow as higher-level evidence is never tested
The department is required to move the person down a grade

questions.hint: Stretch experience is part of progression.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible mix of applications for someone aiming upward?

options.text: Only current-grade roles, until a manager recommends a move
Some current-grade roles and some stretch roles, refining after each
Only stretch roles, so that every attempt carries the highest possible reward
Only roles in the same team, so that the references stay the same

questions.hint: A balance reduces risk and builds evidence.

questions.prompt: Which role could build higher-level evidence without a formal promotion?

options.text: A longer notice period in the current job to build seniority
A temporary promotion or project lead role with wider scope
A change of working pattern with exactly the same duties
A move to a lower grade in a quieter, less demanding team

questions.hint: Temporary or project roles give scope and accountability.

questions.prompt: How should the success profile in a higher-grade advert be used?

options.text: As a set of phrases to copy into the statement of suitability
As a forecast of the exact questions that will be asked at interview
As a checklist of the evidence you need to build
As a statement of the pay you will be offered on appointment

questions.hint: It shows what is assessed at that level.

items.title: L9: Evaluating an advert: fit, risk and red flags
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; GOV.UK, Civil Service Code and Success Profiles
items.body: Before investing time in an application, evaluate the advert as you would a decision. First, fit: do the responsibilities match the work you want and the strengths you have? Second, evidence: can you meet each essential criterion with real examples? Third, practicality: location, pattern, contract type, clearance and start date. Fourth, assessment burden: how many stages and how long will they take? Fifth, risk: what are the signs that the role might not be what it seems? Possible red flags are an advert that is vague about duties, a very high number of essential criteria for a junior grade, a short fixed-term contract with no stated reason, an unusually short closing window, or inconsistent grade, pay and responsibilities. These do not prove a problem; they are reasons to ask the contact. Also notice what the advert does not say, such as who the role reports to or how many posts are available. Ask for the role profile or job description if one is not attached. A good candidate asks a small number of precise questions, such as how the team is structured and what the interview will test, and the answers help to decide. Remember that a role which looks less glamorous may offer better evidence-building for your career. Weigh the decision, and if you decide not to apply, keep a note of why so that you can refine your search criteria.

questions.prompt: An advert for an Administrative Officer role lists fifteen essential criteria, including several that suit a manager. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore the criteria and write a general statement about your skills
Apply anyway, since long lists are normal for junior roles
Assume the grade is wrong and apply for a higher one instead
Ask the contact whether the criteria are correct before deciding

questions.hint: Mismatched criteria is a prompt to check with the department.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful to ask a contact before applying?

options.text: How the team is structured and what the interview assesses
What the pass mark is likely to be for the sift
How many people have already applied for the role
Whether the hiring manager already has a preferred candidate

questions.hint: Precise questions about the work and process help the decision.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a red flag?

options.text: A named contact for questions about the role, with an email address
A very short closing window combined with vague duties
A note explaining how candidates can ask for adjustments
A stated security clearance level that matches the grade of the post

questions.hint: Vague duties and rushed timing deserve questions.

questions.prompt: The advert has no stated reporting line. What is the best response?

options.text: Assume it reports to the head of the department, as most roles do
Treat the gap as a sign that the advert may not be genuine
Leave the question until the interview, when it will be explained
Ask who it reports to, since that shapes the work and development

questions.prompt: A role is less glamorous but offers wider evidence-building. How should a strategic candidate treat it?

options.text: Apply, since less glamorous roles always lead to promotion
Reject it, since it does not match the role you hoped for
Weigh it as a possible stepping stone, not only by appeal
Apply only if no more appealing role has been advertised

questions.hint: Evidence value should be part of the decision.

questions.prompt: Which element would most reduce a candidate's practical ability to take a role?

options.text: Attendance at a distant office for most of the week
A stated closing date and time for applications
A published salary range with a minimum and a maximum
A hybrid pattern with some days working from home

questions.hint: Practical constraints can make a role unworkable.

questions.prompt: If a candidate decides not to apply, what is a useful step?

options.text: Apply anyway in case the decision changes later
Remove the advert from alerts and avoid similar ones
Contact the department to tell them the role is unsuitable
Note why, so the reasons refine future search criteria

questions.hint: Recording reasons helps to refine the search.

questions.prompt: What does 'assessment burden' mean?

options.text: The pay a candidate loses while waiting for a result
The number and length of the stages to complete
The workload the panel carries across the campaign
The cost to the department of running the whole campaign

questions.hint: A heavy assessment needs time and planning.

questions.prompt: A fixed-term role has no stated reason for being temporary. What is sensible?

options.text: Ask the contact why, and what usually happens to post-holders
Assume it will end early, since reasons are not given
Apply without asking, since it makes no difference to the decision
Assume it will turn permanent, since most fixed-term roles do

questions.hint: Understanding the context helps judge risk.

questions.prompt: Why should an applicant ask for the job description if it is not attached?

options.text: It is required by the application form before submission
It guarantees an interview for those who request it
It gives more detail of the duties than the advert summary
It lets the candidate see how other applicants have been assessed

items.title: L9: Running a job search as a portfolio
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: A job search over several months works best as a managed portfolio rather than a series of one-off efforts. Start by setting criteria: grades, locations, professions and working patterns that are acceptable. Then set up alerts and review them at fixed times. Sort vacancies into three groups: strong fit that deserve a full application, possible fit that need a short check, and poor fit to ignore. Space applications so that you can do each well, and try not to have more than a few live at once. Keep a library of examples, each written as a rough STAR outline, tagged with the behaviours they could support. This saves time and keeps quality high, but every answer must be reworded for the question. Track what happens: the number of applications, outcomes at each stage, and common feedback. If you reach interview often but do not get offers, look at interview technique; if you rarely pass the sift, look at written evidence. Allow for the fact that results are not independent, so do not read too much into a single outcome. Plan for the long closing times and the delay between sift and interview. Look after yourself: set a limit on weekly hours, and take breaks after setbacks. Keep your profile and CV current. Review the portfolio monthly and adjust: change your criteria if the market is thin, or widen to adjacent professions.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in managing a search as a portfolio?

options.text: Wait for a manager to suggest which roles suit them
Apply for every vacancy as it appears, to maximise the odds
Set criteria for grades, locations and professions
Choose roles by closing date alone, to keep a steady flow

questions.prompt: Why sort vacancies into strong fit, possible fit and poor fit?

options.text: It removes the need to read each advert in full
It guarantees an interview for roles marked strong fit
It is a step that Civil Service Jobs requires of users
It focuses effort where success and value are likeliest

questions.prompt: Why keep a library of examples tagged by behaviour?

options.text: It lets the same text be pasted into every answer
It saves time if each answer is reworded
It replaces the need to read the advert in detail
It is checked by the panel as part of the sift

questions.hint: A library is a start, not a final answer.

questions.prompt: A candidate reaches interview often but never gets an offer. What does this suggest?

options.text: The written evidence works, but interview technique may not
The written evidence is weak and needs to be rewritten
The reserve list system is not working fairly for them
The sift criteria used by departments are mistaken

questions.hint: Pattern of outcomes points to the weak stage.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to read too much into one outcome?

options.text: Results depend on the field of candidates as well as you
Single outcomes are always wrong and should be disregarded
Outcomes are decided at random by the markers
Panels forget their decisions after a few weeks

questions.prompt: How many live applications is it sensible to have?

options.text: Exactly one at a time, whatever the closing dates
Five at a time, whatever the demands of each one
Only as many as you can prepare to a high standard
As many as possible, since volume is what counts most

questions.prompt: After a setback, which step helps sustain a long search?

options.text: Stop applying for a year to recover from the setbacks
Set a weekly time limit and take breaks
Submit several quick applications to rebuild confidence
Double the hours spent so that momentum is kept up

questions.prompt: If few roles match narrow criteria, what is a sensible adjustment?

options.text: Apply to anything, whatever the fit with your evidence
Lower the standard of applications, to apply for more roles
Stop searching until more roles are advertised
Widen to adjacent professions where evidence transfers

questions.hint: Adjust criteria rather than lower quality.

questions.prompt: What should a monthly review of the portfolio include?

options.text: Applications, outcomes by stage and feedback themes
Only the total number of applications made
A comparison of results with those of colleagues
Only the salaries of the roles that were applied for

questions.prompt: Which is the best reason to keep a profile and CV current?

options.text: The profile determines the sift score for every application
Profile updates are a legal requirement every year
Updates raise the candidate's rank on any reserve list
Vacancies can arrive quickly, so being ready saves time

items.title: L9: Diagnosing repeated sift rejections
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: When a candidate is repeatedly rejected at the sift, the useful question is why. Several causes are common. First, eligibility or essential criteria: perhaps the candidate does not meet the stated requirements. Second, targeting: answers that do not address the behaviour asked about, or that are written generally for all adverts. Third, evidence quality: examples that are vague, lack personal action or have no result. Fourth, scope: examples that are at a lower level than the grade applied for, such as describing routine tasks for a role needing independent judgement. Fifth, presentation: over the word limit, unclear structure, jargon. Sixth, competition: some sifts are simply very competitive. To diagnose, collect scores and feedback from several applications and compare them. If scores cluster just below the pass mark, small improvements may be enough. If scores are very low, the problem is more fundamental, such as mismatched grade or evidence. Test the hypothesis by changing one thing: for example, rewrite the same example with stronger Action and Result, then apply to a similar role. Ask someone experienced, such as a colleague who has sat on panels, to mark an answer against the scoring scale. Look at adverts of a lower grade if the evidence repeatedly does not reach the standard. That is a decision about timing, not a judgement on ability.

questions.prompt: A candidate's scores sit just below the pass mark across several campaigns. What does this suggest?

options.text: The scoring is unfair and should be challenged
Small improvements to evidence may be enough
The candidate should abandon Civil Service applications
The grade is far too high for the evidence held

questions.hint: Close scores suggest a narrow gap.

questions.prompt: Another candidate's scores are very low every time. What is the more likely issue?

options.text: Harsh markers in every department the candidate applies to
A slight weakness in spelling or punctuation
A fundamental mismatch, such as grade or evidence quality
Bad luck in each campaign, with no common cause

questions.hint: Very low scores suggest a larger gap.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a 'targeting' problem?

options.text: Describing a recent example drawn from the candidate's work
Using the STAR structure for each behaviour answer given
Keeping to the word limit that is set for the answer
Writing a general answer that is reused for every advert

questions.hint: Answers must address the specific behaviour asked.

questions.prompt: A candidate applies for a G7 role and describes routine processing tasks. What is the main issue?

options.text: The result is stated too specifically for the marker
The scope of the evidence is below the grade
The candidate used 'I' too often in the answer
The answer contains too much detail about the Action

questions.hint: Evidence must be at the right level.

questions.prompt: What is a sound way to test a hypothesis about your answers?

options.text: Change one thing, such as the Action and Result, then reapply
Change everything at once and apply to a different kind of role
Ask the panel to rescore the earlier answer
Wait a year, then apply again without changes

questions.hint: One change at a time shows what works.

questions.prompt: Who is a useful person to ask to mark an answer?

options.text: A friend who has not read the advert or the scale
The chair of the panel that rejected you
A colleague experienced in sifting, using the scale
A relative who has never worked in the Civil Service

questions.hint: Informed marking against the scale gives useful feedback.

questions.prompt: Why might applying for a lower-grade role be a sensible strategic step?

options.text: It prevents any later stretch applications from being considered
It can build evidence at a recognised standard, as a timing choice
It guarantees promotion at the next campaign
It proves the candidate cannot do the higher role

questions.prompt: Which cause of rejection is outside the candidate's control?

options.text: Choosing the wrong behaviour to write about in the answer
Going over the word limit on one of the answers
Leaving out the Result of the example that was given
A very competitive field that raises the pass mark

questions.prompt: What is the value of comparing feedback across several applications?

options.text: It forces departments to reconsider their decisions
It changes the scores of earlier campaigns
Patterns show what to fix, while one comment is a single view
It allows you to challenge the markers' scores

questions.prompt: Which presentation issue most clearly harms an answer?

options.text: Going over the word limit, so that content may be cut off
Writing in the past tense throughout
Using short paragraphs to separate the stages
Starting with the context of the example

items.title: L9: Reading interview feedback with judgement
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Interview feedback is usually brief, and reading it well takes judgement. Typically it gives scores for each behaviour or strength and some comments. Start with the scores. Note which behaviours scored lowest, but also which were close to the pass mark, as they might be easiest to lift. Read the comments for specifics, such as 'did not explain your own role' or 'gave an example at a lower level than the grade'. Try to link each comment to something in your answer, using your notes. Be careful with generic phrases, like 'others gave stronger examples'. They are true in a competitive campaign and tell you little about what to change. If feedback appears to contradict your sense of how you performed, wait a few days before reacting. If it suggests a factual error, for example that you were scored on the wrong behaviour, you can ask politely for the matter to be reviewed, quoting the evidence. Do not argue about the judgement of a properly run process; instead, ask for clarification if that would help you improve. Remember that a reserve list place shows that you reached the standard. If you were marked down on a strength question, think about whether the role fits your genuine preferences, not just how to answer better. Feedback is a source of information, not a verdict on you.

questions.prompt: What should you look at first in interview feedback?

options.text: The date on which the feedback was sent
The names and grades of the panel members
Scores per behaviour, noting the lowest and near-misses
The length of the written feedback

questions.hint: Scores point to where improvement is most useful.

questions.prompt: Why might a behaviour that was close to the pass mark be a priority?

options.text: A small improvement could make the difference
It proves that the scores were accurate
It shows that the panel disliked the candidate
It is always the most important behaviour for the role

questions.hint: Close scores are cheaper to improve.

questions.prompt: Which feedback comment gives the most useful guidance?

options.text: 'You were not the best candidate on the day'
'Your example did not explain what you personally did'
'Others gave stronger examples in this campaign'
'Better luck next time with another department'

questions.hint: Specific comments show what to change.

questions.prompt: Feedback suggests the panel scored a behaviour that was not in the advert. What is a reasonable step?

options.text: Accept it without asking, since the scores are final
Post a complaint about the panel on social media
Withdraw from all Civil Service applications
Ask politely for a review, quoting the advert

questions.hint: A factual error can be raised calmly.

questions.prompt: What should you avoid doing in response to a properly marked score you disagree with?

options.text: Planning how to improve your next answers
Arguing about the panel's judgement
Asking for clarification of unclear comments
Comparing the feedback with your own notes

questions.hint: Judgement in a properly run process is not a breach.

questions.prompt: Why wait a few days before reacting to feedback that seems wrong?

options.text: Feedback is usually rewritten after a few days
The panel must be given time to confirm it
Initial reactions can distort how you read it
Replies are only accepted a week after it was sent

questions.prompt: What does a reserve list place indicate?

options.text: The candidate will be appointed within a week
The candidate achieved the highest score in the campaign
The candidate was rejected at the interview
The candidate reached the standard for appointment

questions.prompt: If you were marked low on a strengths question, what else might you consider?

options.text: Whether the role really suits your genuine preferences
Whether to avoid strengths-based interviews in future
Whether to invent a strength that sounds more suitable
Whether to complain about strengths-based questions

questions.prompt: Which view of interview feedback is most helpful?

options.text: It is information to learn from, not a verdict on you
It is proof that you should stop applying
It is a source of grounds for a complaint
It is a final ruling on your ability for the Civil Service

questions.prompt: How should you use your own notes when reading feedback?

options.text: Rewrite them so that they match the feedback
Ignore them, since the panel's view is the only one that counts
Link each comment to what you said in the interview
Share them with the panel to challenge the scores

items.title: L9: Internal promotion strategy: evidence at your current grade
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: For a serving civil servant, the best promotion strategy begins in the current role. Promotion panels look for evidence of working at the higher grade, so the aim is to generate that evidence in a fair way. Talk to your line manager early and state your ambition. Ask for stretch tasks that involve wider scope, influence over people outside your team, or ownership of a piece of work. Choose tasks that have a visible outcome, such as leading a small improvement project or coordinating a cross-team piece of work. Keep a record as you go, noting the context, your actions and the results, along with any feedback received. Look at the higher grade's success profile and gaps: if it asks for strategic thinking and you work on detailed casework, look for a way to input into planning. Build relationships through networks and mentoring, which can offer advice and visibility, but visibility is not a substitute for evidence. Be aware that managers cannot guarantee promotion and must follow fair competition. If your manager cannot offer stretch, look elsewhere in the department, or consider a loan or secondment. Review your readiness twice a year against vacancies. When a suitable post is advertised, apply with strong examples and prepare as for any external candidate. Do not assume that being known to the panel is an advantage; the evidence must still be on paper and in the room.

questions.prompt: Which step is the best early move for a civil servant seeking promotion?

options.text: Ask HR to promote them once they feel ready
Tell the line manager of the ambition and ask for stretch
Wait to be noticed, since managers will recommend good staff
Apply to every vacancy immediately to gain interview practice

questions.hint: Starting with the manager sets up evidence-building.

questions.prompt: Which task is most likely to build higher-grade evidence?

options.text: Attending more routine team meetings without a role
Doing more of the same routine casework at a faster pace
Reading the higher grade's job description in more detail
Leading a small improvement project with a visible result

questions.hint: Ownership and visible outcomes show scope.

questions.prompt: Why keep a running record of achievements?

options.text: They are checked by the panel at the interview
Examples are easy to forget and need context and results
They determine pay on appointment
Records are required by the Civil Service Commission

questions.hint: A record makes evidence easier to use.

questions.prompt: What can a manager not do?

options.text: Give feedback on how work compares to the next grade
Offer stretch tasks to people who ask for them
Guarantee promotion, which must follow competition
Support a loan or secondment for a team member

questions.hint: Managers must follow the Recruitment Principles.

questions.prompt: What is the role of networks and mentoring in promotion?

options.text: They give advice but cannot replace evidence
They replace the need to apply for vacancies
They guarantee promotion for those who take part
They allow candidates to skip the sift stage

questions.prompt: If the current manager cannot offer stretch, what is a sensible option?

options.text: Threaten to resign unless stretch tasks are offered
Apply for the manager's own post to gain visibility
Give up the ambition of promotion until a new manager arrives
Look elsewhere in the department, or for a loan or secondment

questions.prompt: How far does being known to the panel help an internal candidate?

options.text: Panels tend to favour candidates they already know, so it is a clear advantage
It helps internal candidates only, since external ones are unknown
Not safely; the evidence must still be shown on paper and in the room
It helps only where the panel members are senior to the candidate

questions.prompt: How should an internal candidate prepare for a promotion interview?

options.text: By asking panel members for hints about the questions
Only by reviewing the department's strategy documents
Lightly, since the panel already knows their work
As rigorously as an external candidate, with strong examples

questions.prompt: How often is it sensible to review readiness against vacancies?

options.text: Never, as readiness is decided by managers
Regularly, such as twice a year
Only when told to do so by HR
Only at the annual appraisal meeting

questions.prompt: Which gap would a person doing detailed casework need to address for a strategic role?

options.text: Evidence of contributing to planning decisions
Evidence of longer service in the same post
A higher volume of casework completed each week
More training in the software used by the team

questions.hint: Match the missing element of the higher profile.

items.title: L9: Lateral move or promotion?
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Professions
items.body: A lateral move, meaning a move to a role at the same grade, can be a better choice than an immediate promotion in some situations. It can widen your experience, for example from operational delivery into policy, or from one profession to another, giving breadth that a promotion panel values. It can move you to a team with better development and clearer stretch. It can also change location or working pattern in a way that supports other priorities. Consider a lateral move when your current role has no route to stretch, when you want to switch professions, or when you want to test a field before committing. A promotion may be better when you have strong evidence at the higher level, when you have an opportunity that suits you, and when the extra responsibility fits your circumstances. Think about what each option leaves you with in two or three years: skills, networks, evidence and opportunities. Consider risks: a lateral move may not pay more, and some specialist moves require learning that delays promotion; a promotion may place you in a role where support is limited. Ask about development, line management and workload. Talk to people who have made similar moves. A lateral move is not a retreat if it is chosen for a purpose. Document your reasons, so you can explain the choice to future panels.

questions.prompt: Which situation most strongly favours a lateral move?

options.text: The person has only recently been promoted into the current grade
The current role has no route to stretch, and the person wants a new profession
The person has strong evidence at the higher grade and a suitable role is advertised
The person simply wants an immediate pay rise as soon as possible

questions.hint: Lateral moves widen experience when current options are limited.

questions.prompt: Which situation most strongly favours a promotion?

options.text: A wish to avoid being assessed in future
A wish to avoid taking on responsibility
A lack of any evidence beyond the current grade
Strong higher-level evidence and a role that fits

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of a lateral move?

options.text: It may not bring more pay, and can delay promotion
It ends the person's Civil Service membership
It reduces the person's grade for a time
It removes pension rights built up so far

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of taking a promotion?

options.text: It always reduces pay, as the post is more demanding
It removes all future development opportunities
The new role may carry heavy responsibility with limited support
It cannot be reversed in any circumstances

questions.prompt: What is a good way to compare options?

options.text: Consider the skills, networks and evidence each leaves you with in two years
Choose the option with the highest immediate pay
Choose the one a friend recommends most strongly
Choose the option with the fewest tasks to learn

questions.prompt: Which questions are useful before a lateral move?

options.text: Questions about the panel's own pay grades
Questions about development, line management and workload
Questions about the total number of applicants
Questions about other candidates' ages and backgrounds

questions.prompt: Why talk to people who have made similar moves?

options.text: They can arrange the appointment on your behalf
They can change the recruitment rules in your favour
They can decide for you which of the options to choose
They can give practical insight into what worked for them

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a lateral move in later applications?

options.text: As a reason to apply only for lower grades in future
As an irrelevant detail to be left off the application
As a deliberate choice, explaining the reasons and learning
As a failure to be hidden from future panels

questions.prompt: Which statement about lateral moves is most accurate?

options.text: They always block later promotion
They are only for those who failed a sift
They are not a retreat if chosen for a purpose
They are always paid more than the earlier post

questions.prompt: Why document your reasons for a move?

options.text: So you can explain the choice to future panels
Because it guarantees acceptance for the next post
Because it changes the pay for the next role
Because HR requires a written reason for each move

items.title: L9: Favouritism, acting-up and internal fairness
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Internal selection can feel less formal, so unfairness may be harder to see. Common risks include favouritism, where a manager gives opportunities to preferred staff; acting-up arrangements that give one person an advantage; vacancies filled without advert when advertising is required; panels containing people with undeclared interests; and informal pressure on who should apply. In a fair process, the vacancy is open to all who might be eligible, criteria are published, candidates are assessed against the same standard, and decisions are recorded. A manager may legitimately recommend that someone is ready to apply, but may not promise a post or pre-select. A candidate who suspects unfairness should first collect facts: what was advertised, who sat on the panel, what happened and when. Then consider the least escalatory route: a conversation with the line manager, a query to HR or the nominated officer, or a formal complaint. Avoid public accusations, which can damage both the process and your own standing. The Civil Service Code supports raising concerns without fear of reprisal, and victimisation of a person for doing so is prohibited. If internal routes do not resolve the issue, the Civil Service Commission can consider whether the Recruitment Principles were breached. Bear in mind that a decision you disagree with is not automatically unfair. Test your concern against the principles of merit, fair and open competition, before acting.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of favouritism in internal selection?

options.text: A manager giving feedback after a sift
A manager explaining the published criteria
A manager encouraging a team member to apply for a vacancy
A manager keeping a developmental post for preferred staff

questions.prompt: What protection does the Civil Service Code offer?

options.text: A right to choose the interview panel
A right to see other candidates' scores
A guarantee of promotion for those who raise concerns
A route to raise concerns without fear of reprisal

items.title: L9: Disclosure and adjustments as a strategy
items.source: Equality Act 2010; GOV.UK, Disability Confident and Access to Work
items.body: For disabled candidates and those with long-term conditions, the decision about whether and when to disclose is personal and strategic. Disclosing at application allows access to the Disability Confident interview offer where the minimum criteria are met, and gives time to arrange adjustments. Not disclosing keeps information private but may mean that adjustments are not available when needed, and the department cannot treat a need it has not been told about as a failure to adjust. Disclosing later, for example after a conditional offer, is often possible, and some people choose to disclose in stages: the minimum needed for the assessment first, and more detail for workplace adjustments later. Whatever the choice, plan the adjustments you would find most useful, and be ready to explain what they do rather than the details of a condition. For tests, consider extra time, alternative formats, assistive software and breaks. For interviews, consider questions in advance, a different format, or a quiet room. For the job itself, consider equipment, flexible hours and working location. Access to Work is a government scheme that can help with the costs of support at work for eligible disabled people; ask about it once you have an offer. Choose a contact you trust, put requests in writing, and record what is agreed. Remember that adjustments exist to enable you to show your ability, not to give an advantage. If adjustments are not provided, raise it quickly and keep records.

questions.prompt: Which is a benefit of disclosing at application?

options.text: Access to the interview offer, and time to arrange adjustments
A guaranteed job offer once the interview is completed
An exemption from pre-employment checks
A higher sift score for candidates who disclose a condition

questions.hint: Early disclosure supports access and planning.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of not disclosing?

options.text: The offer will be withdrawn at the check stage
The department will refuse the application outright
Adjustments may not be in place, as the department cannot know

questions.hint: A department cannot adjust for unknown needs.

questions.prompt: What does staged disclosure mean?

options.text: Disclosing to different people at random

Disclosing only after the first year in post
Sharing the minimum for assessment first, more detail later

questions.prompt: What is it usually more useful to explain to a department?

options.text: The names of all the clinicians involved

At the sift stage

questions.hint: Prompt action helps the department correct it.

items.title: L9: Exceptions to open competition
items.body: The Recruitment Principles require that appointments are made on merit after fair and open competition, but they allow limited exceptions. These are narrow, and each must be used for the reason it exists. Examples include short-term appointments, usually limited to a period of up to about a year, to meet a temporary need; secondments, where a person from another organisation joins for a set period; and certain schemes to help disabled people or others into work. Some exceptions require the department to record the decision and the reasons, and extending a short-term appointment beyond the limit usually requires further approval. The aim is flexibility without undermining fairness. If an exception is overused, it can become a way of avoiding competition. A person who is appointed through an exception does not usually gain a right to a permanent post, and permanent appointment still needs a fair and open competition. If you are offered a short-term appointment, ask how long it will last, whether it can be extended, and what route to permanency exists. If you are a candidate who feels that repeated short-term appointments are being used to avoid fair competition, you can raise it with the department and, if needed, the Civil Service Commission. For anyone involved in recruitment, the practical rule is: if you are unsure whether an exception applies, ask HR, because getting it wrong can breach the Principles.

items.title: L9: Negotiating start dates, location and working pattern
items.source: GOV.UK, Flexible working; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: After an offer, there are often practical points to settle: the start date, the base location, and the working pattern. Some are fixed by the post, and some can be discussed. Start dates are often flexible within limits, since the department needs the role filled but must wait for checks and your notice. Offer a realistic date, explain your notice, and avoid committing before you know your employer's position. Location is usually fixed by the advert, though some roles list several offices and the department may consider a preference. Working pattern is more flexible: many Civil Service roles can be done part-time, as a job share or compressed hours, and hybrid arrangements are common though they vary. Employees have a statutory right to request flexible working, and under changes in recent years this right applies from the first day of employment, though the employer may refuse for set business reasons. Before asking, think about what you want and what the employer needs, and propose a pattern that works for both. Put requests in writing. Be honest about constraints, such as caring responsibilities, and consider offering a trial period. Do not make demands that the role cannot meet; if the role needs on-site working, a request that ignores this is likely to fail. If a request is refused, ask for the reason and whether an alternative would work. Keep the discussion positive and record what is agreed.

questions.prompt: Which element of an offer is usually most flexible?

options.text: The start date, within the limits of checks and notice
The grade shown on the advert for the post
The department that the role is based in
The security clearance level that is needed

options.text: Make a formal complaint immediately

options.text: It increases pay during the trial

items.title: L9: Probation, settling in and building a reputation
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Code
items.body: The first months in a new role matter. Many Civil Service posts include a probation period, often several months, though length and rules vary by department and by whether you are a new entrant or have moved within the Civil Service. During probation, performance, conduct and attendance are reviewed, with regular meetings. The aim is mutual: you learn the role, and the department checks fit. Start by clarifying expectations with your line manager: objectives, standards, and how performance is assessed. Ask what a good first three months looks like. Learn the team's systems and the Civil Service Code, including your duties around confidentiality and impartiality. Build relationships with colleagues and stakeholders, and ask questions early rather than guessing. Keep a record of what you have achieved, as it will support your first review and later applications. Seek feedback, and act on it visibly. If something is not working, such as unclear duties or difficulty with a task, raise it quickly with your manager rather than hoping it resolves. If you need adjustments, or have caring commitments that affect working patterns, discuss them at the start. Do not take on so much that quality drops. If a promotion or move is your goal, treat the new role as an opportunity to show reliability first, because a strong reputation helps future applications. Be aware that a poor start can be recovered with honesty and a plan, and that support, such as a mentor or buddy, is often available.
